title: At the café and the restaurant
topic: ordering and paying; boire; definite vs partitive article
why: After shopping, it's time to sit down: this lesson gives you everything to order and pay at a café or a restaurant, from un café to l'addition, plus the verb boire. It also settles the key contrast of the unit: J'aime le fromage, but je prends du fromage.

At the café

The French café has its own vocabulary, and a few words don't mean what an English speaker expects.

FrenchEnglish
un caféan espresso (small, strong, black)
un crème (un café crème)a coffee with hot milk
un décaa decaf
un théa tea
un chocolat chauda hot chocolate
un jus d'orangean orange juice
une pressiona draft beer
une carafe d'eaua jug of tap water (free)

Ordering

You have three polite ways to order: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. / Pour moi, un thé. / Je vais prendre un crème. The last one uses aller + infinitive, a future form you'll study in unit 6: take it as a fixed phrase for now. Waiters and customers say vous to each other, and you call the waiter with Monsieur !, Madame ! or S'il vous plaît !

Boire

boire
jebois
tubois
il, elle, onboit
nousbuvons
vousbuvez
ils, ellesboivent

Three stems: boi- in the singular, buv- for nous and vous, boiv- for ils. The singular forms all sound the same, like “bwa”.

If you want a longer black coffee, ask for un café allongé; a big milky one is un grand crème. And never call the waiter “garçon”: it's old-fashioned and sounds rude today.

", "

At the restaurant

Two famous false friends are waiting for you on the table.

FrenchEnglishCareful!
la cartethe menu (the list of dishes)La carte, s'il vous plaît.
le menuthe set menu (fixed price)le menu à 22 euros: starter, main course and dessert
l'entréethe starter, the appetizerIn American English, the “entrée” is the main course!
le platthe main course; the dishle plat du jour = today's special
le dessertthe dessertune tarte, une crème brûlée…
l'additionthe checkL'addition, s'il vous plaît !

How do you like your steak?

The waiter asks Quelle cuisson ? French steaks are cooked less than in the US or the UK:

  • bleu: very rare, almost raw
  • saignant: rare (literally “bleeding”)
  • à point: medium
  • bien cuit: well done

A carafe of tap water is free: just ask for une carafe d'eau. Bottled water is de l'eau plate (still) or de l'eau gazeuse (sparkling).

In France the service charge is included in the prices: that's what service compris means on the menu. A tip (un pourboire) is a small extra, a few coins for good service, never a fixed percentage.

", "

J'aime le fromage, je prends du fromage

This is the key contrast of the unit. With verbs of taste (aimer, adorer, détester, préférer), you talk about a thing in general, so French uses le, la, les. With verbs of consumption (prendre, boire, manger, vouloir, acheter), you talk about some of it, so you use du, de la, des. English uses no article in either case.

In generalSome
J'aime le fromage. (I like cheese.)Je prends du fromage. (I'll have some cheese.)
Elle adore le vin rouge.Elle boit du vin rouge.
Je déteste la bière.Je ne bois pas de bière.
Tu préfères les frites ?Tu veux des frites ?

Look at the third line: in the negative, the partitive becomes de (pas de bière), but the general article stays: Je n'aime pas la bière.

Je n'aime pas le poisson, alors je prends du poulet.I don't like fish, so I'll have some chicken.
Les enfants boivent du lait, mais ils détestent le café !The children drink milk, but they hate coffee!

A quick test: if you could add “in general” in English, use le, la, les. If you could add “some”, use du, de la, des.
